doc.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017

title: Jazz today: Newark partnerships and the museum-music fear
summary: Pelote describes the Institute's partnerships with NJPAC, WGBO and others, and fears jazz is becoming museum music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Close enough for jazz. Oh, I love talking to you. I’m not sure I can phrase this question, to sort of wrap up. You know we’ve been talking about the past and what’s your take on jazz in America now, considering record sales and jazz education and jazz as an art form. © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

It’s all over the place right now. You know it’s interesting that you ask me the question because one of the thing that Ed and I — Ed Berger — I keep bringing his name up and I guess it’s because his death is still so fresh in my head. But he used to talk about the fact that we have this chancellor in Newark now, I used to say she’s new but she’s been here for a couple of years ago so she’s not that new anymore. And she’s been trying to use the Institute of Jazz Studies as a sort of a way to, I don’t know, to like connect with some of the other cultural organizations in Newark. So we’ve been partnering with NJPAC for some things. We we’ve always kind of did that but now it’s more so that that’s happening, in their jazz program. And also the Newark Museum and the Library and other groups similar. And so she sees jazz as kind of a way to bring more notoriety to the Institute, and to Rutgers University, and also as a fundraising mechanism, which is interesting because jazz sales and the popularity of jazz, also WGBO is another institution in Newark that we’re trying to kind of partner more with. And we always have sort of partnered with them — they used to have a show called Jazz From the Archives for years, before they canceled us. So really I see jazz as doing a lot of different things. I mean the fear that it’s going to become a museum music, it’s still very much there. Because we were talking last night about Fats Navarro and Clifford Brown and Kenny Dorham and stuff like that. And we looked at each other and said we sat around, a bunch of old farts sitting around talking about the good old days. Like the kids today don’t know who these people are today. I mean what are we doing here you know. Is this what jazz is now? Just a bunch of old recordings? So there’s that fear. But, you know, I also Thursday, last Thursday before coming down here Valery Ponomarev, the Russian trumpeter. I always mess up his last name. He had a group of kids NJPAC has something called Jazz for Teens.
